The Libertarian Party, founded in 1971. It is the longest-standing active third party in the United States, advocating for minimal government intervention in both economics and personal liberties. Drawing votes primarily from disaffected Republicans and fiscally conservative independents, the party has run a presidential candidate in every general election since 1972, though its electoral impact has remained limited.

The party emerged from a coalition of libertarian intellectuals, followers of the Ludwig von Mises Institute, and supporters of Ron Paul frustrated by both major parties' interventionism and military hawkishness. Libertarian presidential candidates have included Roger MacBride in 1976, Ed Clark in 1980, Harry Browne in 1996 and 2000, and Gary Johnson in 2012 and 2016. Johnson's 2016 campaign attracted nearly 3.3 percent of the popular vote, the party's strongest showing to date.

The party opposes most government regulation and taxation, favors drug legalization, and advocates for non-interventionist foreign policy. It champions individual liberty across social and economic dimensions. Despite never winning a presidential election, Libertarians have elected several candidates to state legislatures and local office, establishing a modest but persistent institutional presence.

The party functions as a pressure valve for Republican-leaning voters frustrated with social conservatism or military spending, and for Democratic-leaning voters hostile to economic regulation. Yet internal factions dispute pragmatism, seeking state-level wins and influence, versus purism, demanding ideological consistency on property rights and non-aggression. These disagreements cause recurring splits. The Libertarian Party remains the most durable active third party in modern U.S. politics.
